To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the LMW serum fraction contains over 340 proteins, that the LMW fraction can be enriched by centrifugal ultrafiltrate of serum, and that the fractionation and identification of the LMW fraction is amenable to mass spectrometry-based proteomic analyses.

centrifugal ultrafiltrations under conditions that disrupt protein-protein interactions, followed by digestion with trypsin and strong cation exchange fractionation, is a simple, rapid, and effective method for the isolation of the low molecular weight (10 kDa) serum proteome for subsequent analysis by mass spectrometry.

we have identified a large number of low molecular weight human serum proteins by a combination of centrifugal ultrafiltrations, trypsin digestion, strong cation exchange fractionation, and microcapillary reversed phase chromatography coupled on line with tandem mass spectrometric analysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of analytical methodologies for the analysis of the low molecular weight serum proteome and the identification of proteins and protein fragments present in this fraction.
developing a comprehensive understanding of the human serum proteome, which may ultimately lead to the development of a diagnostic tool to detect early stage disease.
developing a method for the enrichment of LMW proteins and peptides for subsequent analysis by mass spectrometry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LMW serum protein/peptide sample is an enriched source of low abundance proteins and peptides that are present at concentrations that allow for their detection and identification by tandem mass spectrometric methods.
the method of centrifugal ultrafiltrations is an effective and simple means of enriching the LMW fraction of human serum and can be applied to the analysis of other biological fluids.
the centrifugal ultra-filtration of serum under solvent conditions that disrupt protein-protein interactions is effective at enriching the LMW proteome for mass spectrometric analysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the LMW proteome of human serum can be characterized by mass spectrometry without the need for extensive prefractionation, thus providing a valuable resource for the discovery of novel disease biomarkers and for the elucidation of the molecular basis of protein-protein binding in the circulatory system.

the use of solvent conditions to disrupt protein-protein interactions during ultrafiltration resulted in a sample that was devoid of albumin and other high molecular weight proteins while still retaining many of the LMW protein species.
the LMW serum sample is a complex mixture of small proteins, peptides, and small molecule metabolites that is amenable to proteomic analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the serum proteome is a dynamic system that can be fractionated into distinct sub-proteomes.

the LMW fraction of serum carries a rich proteomic archive, and the removal of the high abundance serum proteins by centrifugal ultrafiltraton is a simple and effective means for the enrichment and analysis of this proteomic archive.
serum albumin is an excellent carrier protein, but it does not bind to the majority of the low molecular weight proteins and peptides in serum.
